chapter_name: Sketching, Still Life and Object Drawing
learning_objective: 🎯 Master the skill of observation! Learn to draw everyday objects realistically by understanding light, shadow, and proportion.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Still life is the drawing or painting of inanimate (non-moving) objects arranged together, such as fruits, vases, books, or bottles. It teaches artists how to observe carefully.
Proportion is the size relationship between different objects. Artists often use their pencil held at arm's length to measure and compare the height and width of objects before drawing.

To make a flat drawing look 3D, you must add shading. You need to identify the light source. The side facing the light gets a 'Highlight', and the opposite side gets a 'Core Shadow' and casts a 'Cast Shadow' on the table.
Artists use different pencil marks to create shadows: Hatching (parallel lines), Cross-hatching (intersecting lines), Stippling (dots), and Blending (smooth transitions).
Placing one object partially in front of another creates 'overlapping'. This is the simplest way to create an illusion of depth (3D space) on a 2D piece of paper.

fun_activity.title: 🔦 The Shadow Play
fun_activity.instructions: Place a mug and an apple on a table in a dark room. Shine a flashlight on them from different angles (left, right, top). Observe how the shadows stretch, shrink, and move depending on the light source!

exam_tips: 📌 Always outline the basic geometric shapes of objects lightly before adding details.
📌 Remember the shading sequence: Highlight -> Midtone -> Core Shadow -> Reflected Light -> Cast Shadow.
📌 Proportion is crucial; compare the sizes of objects to one another (e.g., 'Is the apple half the height of the vase?').
quick_recap: ⭐ Still life improves an artist's observational skills and understanding of forms.
⭐ Shading gives a two-dimensional drawing the illusion of three-dimensional volume.
⭐ Cross-hatching is an excellent technique for creating dark, textured shadows with a pencil.
